title: Hazard-Signature Tombstones: Commit-Time Forget Lockout for LLM Agent Memory

contributions.purpose: Formalize the paraphrase re-injection vulnerability in LLM agent memory deletion and show naive deletion backfires.
contributions.mechanism: Define the paraphrase re-injection attack (adversary re-inserts semantically equivalent paraphrases of deleted records under new IDs) and measure ID-based deletion under it.
contributions.evaluation: Naive ID-delete increases poisoned retrieval proportion (PRP@3) from 0.67 (no forget) to 0.94 as 50 paraphrases flood the index after 10 poisoned records are removed (a 40% increase).
contributions.domain: Security of persistent LLM agent memory (memory poisoning / deletion)
contributions.source_quote: We formalize the paraphrase re-injection problem for LLM agent memory and demonstrate that naive ID-based deletion is counterproductive, increasing poisoned retrieval by 40%.

contributions.purpose: Prevent paraphrased re-injection of deleted harmful content at commit time.
contributions.mechanism: Hazard-Signature Tombstones (HST): extract discrete hazard signatures (LLM-classified structured labels over a fixed taxonomy) from deleted records, store as tombstone keys, and block incoming writes via fuzzy set-containment matching (H_w subset-of/superset-of H_t).
contributions.evaluation: Fuzzy set-containment raises hazard-signature stability across paraphrases to 92% vs 30% for exact matching.
contributions.domain: Commit-time forget/lockout policy for agent memory stores
contributions.source_quote: We propose HST with fuzzy set-containment matching, achieving 92% hazard-signature stability across paraphrases compared to 30% with exact matching.

contributions.purpose: Demonstrate HST eliminates poisoned retrieval without harming benign retrieval.
contributions.mechanism: Evaluate HST against ID-delete and retrieval-time exact/fuzzy filtering baselines on the MemoryGraft corpus (100 benign + 10 poisoned, 50 paraphrases, BGE-M3 + FAISS), measuring PRP@3, benign recall, write-block rate, false blocks.
contributions.evaluation: HST achieves PRP@3 = 0.0 with Benign Recall@3 = 1.0, WriteBlockRate = 1.0, and only 3% benign false-positive rate; retrieval-time fuzzy also reaches PRP@3=0.0 but drops benign recall to 0.97 due to slot wasting; result robust across embedding backends.
contributions.domain: Defense evaluation for RAG/agent memory poisoning
contributions.source_quote: We demonstrate that HST achieves complete poisoned elimination (PRP@3 = 0.0) while preserving perfect benign recall (1.0), blocking 100% of paraphrased re-injection attempts with only 3% false positive rate.

self_declared_provenance.quote: We draw inspiration from distributed systems, particularly the Observed-Remove Set (OR-Set) (Bieniusa et al., 2012), a conflict-free replicated data type that uses tombstones to mark deleted elements. Unlike OR-Set's exact-match tombstones, HST employs fuzzy semantic matching to handle paraphrased re-injections.
However, unlike OR-Set's exact-match tombstones over element identifiers, HST tombstones operate over semantic hazard signatures.
Our work differs by operating at commit time with semantic matching, preventing index pollution rather than filtering at retrieval.
We evaluate HST on a memory poisoning scenario using the MemoryGraft corpus (Srivastava & He, 2025), which contains 100 benign and 10 poisoned experience records.
